Spoken_Languages_English_Disciplines_Mat.description:
This case study is similar to the one we worked on in the Arrays lesson. However, here we will utilize functions in order to better organize the code. This case study also includes a few extra requirements and might be a bit more difficult than the one in the Arrays lesson.

Context

You want to teach your little siblings some math in a fun way. You want them to think of any three integers then try to figure out the result of either multiplying or adding each pair of numbers from the four integers. You also want your siblings to be able to verify their answers.

Task

Create a function named learnMath that receives three arguments:

  • An array of three integers, named nums, that includes the numbers you want to practice on.
  • A string, named operation, that may have one of two values: "add" or "multiply".
  • A string, named type, that may have one of two values: "questions" or "answers".

For each combination of two integers from nums, the function should do the following:

Spoken_Languages_English.body:
Introduction

When writing a program, you can decide which statements to execute based on certain conditions.

For example, informing users whether they are adults based on their age. The algorithm could be something like this:

Read user's age.
IF age is at least 18, THEN display "Adult".

In the above algorithm, displaying the message is controlled by the condition. Only if the condition is true will the word Adult be displayed.

You can use any of the following mechanisms to implement decision making in your program:

Programming_Languages_Python_Spoken_Lang.body:
1. if statement.
  2. Conditional operator.
  3. switch statement.
  1. if statement.
  2. Conditional operator.

Programming_Languages_Java_Spoken_Langua.body:
1. if statement.
  2. Conditional operator.
  3. switch statement.

Spoken_Languages_English.body:
if Statement

The if statement uses conditions to perform different actions for different decisions. We have the following options for writing an if statement:

Programming_Languages_Java_Spoken_Langua.body:
1. if
  2. else
  3. else if
  4. nested if

Programming_Languages_Python_Spoken_Lang.body:
1. if
  2. else
  3. elif
  4. nested if

1) if statement

An if statement executes a block of code if a condition is true. If the condition is false, no alternative is provided. The condition is a boolean expression that evaluates to either True or False.

if condition:
    # one or more statements to execute if condition is true

Programming_Languages_Java_Spoken_Langua.body:
1) if statement

An if statement executes a block of code if a condition is true. If the condition is false, no alternative is provided. The condition is a boolean expression that evaluates to either true or false.

if (condition){
    //one or more statements to execute if condition is true
}

The braces { } above can be omitted if they enclose a single statement:

if (condition)
    //one statement to execute if condition is true

Programming_Languages_Python_Spoken_Lang.body:
Note that all statements executed based on the condition should have the same indentation.

if condition:
    # statement 1
    # statement 2
    # ...

Spoken_Languages_English.body:
Example

The code below prints Adult if age is at least 18, then the code prints "Goodbye!"

Programming_Languages_Python_Spoken_Lang.body:
age = input("How old are you?")
age = int(age)
if age &gt= 18:
    print("Adult")
print("Goodbye!")

Programming_Languages_Java_Spoken_Langua.body:
Let’s trace the code to see how it works:

  • Lines 1 to 3 read the value of age from the user as an integer.
  • Line 4 tests a condition of whether age is at least 18 using the >= operator (larger than or equal).
    • If the condition is true, line 5 is executed, printing the word Adult.
    • If condition is false,  line 5 is skipped.
  • Line 6 prints Goodbye! regardless of the condition (because line 7 is outside the if-statement).

Programming_Languages_Python_Spoken_Lang.body:
Let’s trace the code to see how it works:

  • Lines 1 and 2 read the value of age from the user as an integer.
  • Line 2 tests a condition of whether age is at least 18 using the >= operator (larger than or equal).
    • If the condition is True, line 4 is executed, printing the word Adult.
    • If condition is False,  line 4 is skipped.
  • Line 5 prints Goodbye! regardless of the condition (because line 7 is outside the if-statement).

Programming_Languages_Java_Spoken_Langua.body:
if (condition){
    //statement(s) to execute if condition is true
} else {
    //statement(s) to execute if condition is false
}

Programming_Languages_Python_Spoken_Lang.body:
if condition:
    # statement(s) to execute if condition is True
else:
    # statement(s) to execute if condition is False

Spoken_Languages_English.body:
2) else statement

An else statement allows adding an optional block to an if statement in order to provide an alternative path in case the condition is false.

Programming_Languages_Java_Spoken_Langua.body: Similarly to earlier, braces { } can be omitted if they enclose a single statement:

Spoken_Languages_English.body:
Example

Let's extend our example from the previous section by displaying something different if the condition is false.

Example

Let's extend our example from the previous section by displaying something different if the condition is false.

Programming_Languages_Python_Spoken_Lang.body:
age = input("How old are you? ")
age = int(age)
if age &gt= 18:
    print("Adult")
else:
    print("Not Adult") 
print("Goodbye!")

Programming_Languages_Java_Spoken_Langua.body:
Now, let’s trace the code to see how it works:

  • Lines 1 to 3 read the value of age from the user as an integer.
  • Line 4 tests whether age is greater than or equal to 18.
    • If true, line 5 is executed, printing Adult, and lines 5 and 6 are skipped.
    • If false,  line 5 is skipped, and line 7 is executed, printing Not Adult.

  • Line 8 is executed regardless of the condition because it is outside the if..else statement.

Programming_Languages_Python_Spoken_Lang.body:
Now, let’s trace the code to see how it works:

  • Lines 1 and 2 read the value of age from the user as an integer.
  • Line 3 tests whether age is greater than or equal to 18.
    • If True, line 4 is executed, printing Adult, and lines 5 and 6 are skipped.
    • If False,  line 4 is skipped, and line 6 is executed, printing Not Adult.

  • Line 7 is executed regardless of the condition because it is outside the if..else statement.

Programming_Languages_Java_Spoken_Langua.body:
3) else if statement

An else if statement allows for checking additional conditions if the previous conditions were false.

if (condition1){
    //statement(s) to execute if condition1 is true
} else if (condition2){
    //statement(s) to execute if condition 1 is false and condition 2 is true
} else if (condition3){
    //statement(s) to execute if conditions 1,2 are false and condition 3 is true
...
} else {
    //statem..ent(s) to execute if all above conditions are false
}

Programming_Languages_Python_Spoken_Lang.body:
3) elif statement

An elif (else if) statement allows for checking additional conditions if the previous conditions were false.

if condition1:
    # statement(s) to run if condition1 is true
elif condition2:
    # statement(s) to run if condition 1 is false and condition 2 is true
elif condition3:
    # statement(s) to run if conditions 1,2 are false and condition 3 is true
...
else:
    # statement(s) to run if all above conditions are false

Spoken_Languages_English.body: Example: let's further extend our age example from before to print different messages based on the age group.

Programming_Languages_Python_Spoken_Lang.body:
age = input("How old are you? ")
age = int(age)
if age &gt= 65:
    print("Senior")
elif age &gt= 18:
    print("Adult")
elif age &gt= 12:
    print("Teen")
else
    print("Child")
print("Goodbye!")

Let’s trace the code to see how it works:

  • Lines 1,2: read user's age.
  • Lines 3 to 10: coniditions are checked from top to bottom; once a condition is found True, code under that condition is executed, then program jumps outside if statement straight to line 11. If all conditions were False, code under else is executed. 
    • for example, assume age is 20. The condition in Line 3 is checked first and found to be False. Therefore, the condition in line 5 is checked next. As this condition is True, Line 6 is executed, printing Adult, then the program control jumps to Line 11.

  • Line 11 is executed regardless of all conditions, again because it is outside the if statement.

Programming_Languages_Java_Spoken_Langua.body:
Let’s trace the code to see how it works:

  • Lines 1 to 3: read user's age.
  • Lines 4 to 11: coniditions are checked from top to bottom; once a condition is found true, code under that condition is executed, then program jumps outside if statement straight to line 12. If all conditions were false, code under else is executed. 
    • for example, assume age is 20. The condition in Line 4 is checked first and found to be false. Therefore, the condition in line 6 is checked next. As this condition is true, Line 7 is executed, printing Adult, then the program control jumps to Line 12.

  • Line 12 is executed regardless of all conditions, again because it is outside the if statement.

Spoken_Languages_English.body:
(1) while Loops

A while loop repeats a block of code as long as a given condition is true. The general syntax for a while loop is:

    //loop body (statements to be repeated)

Spoken_Languages_English.body: Like an if statement, the code inside the while loop will only run if the condition is true. However, after executing the code, the condition is checked again; if it is still true, the loop body is executed again, and so on. If the condition is false, the program continues to the next code block right after the loop body.

Spoken_Languages_French.body: Comme une instruction if, le code à l'intérieur de la "while loop" ne s'exécutera que si la condition est vraie. Cependant, après l'exécution du code, la condition est à nouveau vérifiée ; s'il est toujours vrai, le corps de la boucle est exécuté à nouveau, et ainsi de suite. Si la condition est fausse, le programme passe au bloc de code suivant juste après le corps de la boucle.

Précision de l'Floating Point

Comme vous le savez peut-être, les ordinateurs utilisent le format binaire (0 et 1) pour représenter les données. Cela inclut bien sûr les données numériques. Cette représentation fonctionne bien pour les nombres entiers. Cependant, il échoue parfois à représenter avec précision les fractions. Par exemple, le code suivant devrait imprimer 1.2 dans les deux instructions, n'est-ce pas ? Cependant, la sortie réelle de la deuxième instruction est 1,2000000000000002.

Spoken_Languages_English.body:
Floating Point Accuracy

As you may know, computers use binary format (0's and 1's) to represent data. This of course includes numeric data. This representation works well for whole numbers. However, it sometimes fails to accurately represent fractions. For example, the following code is expected to print 1.2 in both statements, right? However, the actual output of the second statement is 1.2000000000000002.

Programming_Languages_Java.body:
System.out.println(1.2);        //output: 1.2
System.out.println(1.1 + 0.1);  //output: 1.2000000000000002

Spoken_Languages_English.body:
Where does this inaccuracy come from? This brings us back to the way computers represent data in binary (0 and 1). Many decimal fractions are approximated when stored in computers. The value 0.1 is represented in binary using a very long sequence 0.000110011001100110... which must be approximated in order to store it in computer memory.

A nice analogy is when you (human) want to write the fraction 2/3 as a decimal number. You will have to write 0.66666666666.. which is infinitely long, and you can only approximate it to something like 0.66667. The computer does the same thing with decimal fractions.

Why is this important to know here? As seen in the code above, the result of 1.1 + 0.1 is not equal to 1.2. Knowing that now, you should NOT use floating-point values with equality checking in loop condition.

Call Stacks

How does the program keep track of which method is running, what variables are being used, and where the flow of execution must continue from after each call? All of these tasks are handled by the call stack. The call stack consists of stack frames, one for each method call, containing values for local variables, the return address, etc.

For instance, when the main() method is called, it is added to the call stack. All global variables are contained in its stack frame.

Here is an illustration of the call stack after each method call in the above code:

Toutes ces tâches sont gérées par la pile d'appels. La pile d'appels se compose de cadres de pile, un pour chaque appel de méthode, contenant des valeurs pour les variables locales, l'adresse de retour, etc.

Introduction

In this lesson, we will learn about recursion which is a very powerful problem solving technique.

Recursion is a powerful technique for solving complicated problems by breaking them into smaller and more managable problems. Recursion involves a function calling itself within its own definition. In fact, such a function is called a recursive function.

In recursion, a function solves a base case (typically, the simplest version of the problem) directly and then calls itself with a modified input to solve a smaller version of the original problem. This process continues until the base case is reached, at which point the function returns a value. The recursive calls build upon each other, gradually solving larger instances of the problem until the original problem is solved.

Example

Spoken_Languages_French.body:
Introduction

Dans cette leçon, nous allons apprendre la récursivité, une technique très puissante pour résoudre des problèmes.

La récursivité est une technique puissante pour résoudre des problèmes compliqués en les décomposant en problèmes plus petits et plus gérables. La récursivité implique qu'une fonction s'appelle elle-même dans sa propre définition. En fait, une telle fonction est appelée une fonction récursive.

En récursivité, une fonction résout un cas de base (généralement, la version la plus simple du problème) directement, puis s'appelle avec une entrée modifiée pour résoudre une version plus petite du problème original. Ce processus continue jusqu'à ce que le cas de base soit atteint, moment auquel la fonction retourne une valeur. Les appels récursifs se construisent les uns sur les autres, résolvant progressivement des instances plus grandes du problème jusqu'à ce que le problème original soit résolu.

Exemple

Voici un exemple d'une méthode qui imprime n nombres dans l'ordre décroissant.

Spoken_Languages_English.body: Let's try to trace the code for n = 3.

Spoken_Languages_French.body: Essayons de tracer le code pour n = 3.

Spoken_Languages_English.body: And thus, we end up with 3 2 1 on the console. The above example also shows us the importance of having a stopping condition (base case) -- otherwise the code would have gone into an infinite loop. When n becomes non-positive, the recursive stacking stops and thus, the base case for this recursion is n <= 0.

Spoken_Languages_French.body: Et ainsi, nous obtenons 3 2 1 sur la console. Cet exemple montre également l'importance d'avoir une condition d'arrêt (cas de base) - sinon, le code aurait pu entrer dans une boucle infinie. Lorsque n devient non positif, l'empilement récursif s'arrête et donc, le cas de base pour cette récursivité est n <= 0.

Penser de manière récursive

Dans cette leçon, nous allons parcourir le processus de réflexion de manière récursive sur un problème.

En regardant le dernier exemple de la fonction print, on pourrait se demander pourquoi nous avons même besoin de la récursivité si nous pouvons simplement utiliser des boucles ? Apparemment, chaque code récursif peut être écrit comme un code itératif (en utilisant des boucles) et vice versa. Cependant, la récursivité simplifie souvent considérablement le problème que nous voulons résoudre, tandis que cela aurait pu être beaucoup plus difficile en utilisant l'itération.

Penser de manière récursive implique trois étapes cruciales :

  1. Identifier l'appel récursif (c'est-à-dire la forme plus simple)
  2. Identifier les conditions d'arrêt en identifiant le(s) cas de base(s)
  3. Écrire la méthode récursive

Les solutions récursives sont beaucoup plus intuitives et plus simples à comprendre. Dans cette section, nous allons aborder un problème qui semble assez compliqué et nous essaierons de le résoudre en utilisant la récursivité.

Énoncé du problème

Trouver le nombre de chemins pour atteindre le coin inférieur droit d'une grille m x n en se déplaçant uniquement vers la droite ou vers le bas à chaque étape donnée.

Avant de plonger dans le codage, analysons d'abord le problème pour certaines valeurs de m et n. À titre d'illustration, considérons le cas où m = 3 et n = 2. Nous voulons trouver le nombre de façons d'atteindre la fin en se déplaçant uniquement vers la droite ou vers le bas.


Il n'est pas difficile de voir que le nombre de chemins dans ce cas est de 4, comme illustré ci-dessous :


Pouvons-nous réduire le problème à un problème plus petit ? Remarquez que pour atteindre la position finale, nous devons soit atteindre la position juste au-dessus de la position finale, soit la position à gauche de la position finale. Ainsi, nous pouvons dire que le nombre de chemins différents pour atteindre la fin est égal à la somme du nombre de chemins pour atteindre les positions à gauche et au-dessus de la fin.

Soit f(m,n) le nombre de chemins du début à la fin. Ainsi, selon la discussion ci-dessus,

f(m, n) = f(m, n-1) + f(m-1, n)

Nous avons donc une idée de comment les appels récursifs vont fonctionner - nous retournons simplement f(m, n-1) + f(m-1, n). Mais, quelle devrait être notre condition d'arrêt (cas de base) ? À chaque étape, la taille de la grille diminue (c'est là l'essence de la résolution de problèmes récursive ; les problèmes plus petits s'accumulent pour résoudre des problèmes plus grands !) et donc, nous atteindrons un stade où nous aurons seulement besoin du nombre de chemins dans une grille m x 1 ou 1 x n. De toute évidence, dans ce cas, la réponse sera simplement 1 car il n'y a qu'une seule route : aller uniquement vers la droite ou uniquement vers le bas en fonction des dimensions de la grille. Ainsi, nous avons

f(m, 1) = f(1, n) = 1

et ceci pourrait être notre cas de base. Voici le code complet pour ce problème :

Spoken_Languages_English.body:
Thinking Recursively

In this lesson, we will walkthrough the process of thinking recursively on a problem.

Looking at the last example of the print function, one might wonder why we even need recursion when we can use loops. In fact, any recursive code can be rewritten as iterative code using loops (and the opposite is also true!). However, recursion might simplify some problems significantly. Solving some problems with iteration might be much more challenging and require more code, but will be much more efficient. So, both approaches have their place, but knowing how to think recursively is very helpful!

Thinking recursively involves three crucial steps:

  1. Identify the recursive call (i.e. the simpler form)
  2. Identify stopping condition(s) by identifying base case(s)
  3. Write the recursive method

Recursive solutions are much more intuitive and simpler to understand. In this section, we will walk through a seemingly complex problem and we will try to solve it using recursion.

Problem Statement

Find number of paths to reach from top left corner in a m x n grid to the lower bottom corner by either moving right or below at each given step.

Before we dive into coding, let us first analyze the problem for some value of m and n. For sake of illustration, let us consider the case when m = 3 and n = 2. We wish to find number of ways to reach from start to end by either moving right or down.


It's not hard to see that the number of paths in this case is 4 as shown below


Can we reduce the problem to a smaller one? Note that to reach the end position, we must either reach the position above the end position or the position left of the end position. Thus, we can say that the number of different paths reaching the "end" is equal to the sum of the number of ways to reach positions above it and to its left.

Let f(m,n) be the number of paths from start to end. Thus, by the above discussion:

f(m, n) = f(m, n-1) + f(m-1, n)

This gives us an idea of how the recursive calls are going to work -- we simply return f(m, n-1) + f(m-1, n). But, what should be our stopping condition (also known as the Base case)? Well, at each step, the size of grid is getting smaller (this is the essence of recursive problem solving; smaller problems build up to solve bigger ones!) and thus, we will reach a point when we just need the number of paths in a m x 1 or 1 x n grid. Obviously, in both these case, the answer is going to be 1 because there is only one route: going either only right or only down, respectively. Thus, we have

f(m, 1) = f(1, n) = 1

and this could be our base case. We now have our solution in theory! Writing the code is the easy part:

Spoken_Languages_English.body: The above illustration shows us how powerful recursion can be. A problem that might have seemed complex can be solved in 3 lines of code! The key steps to solving any problem in a recursive manner are to first spilt the problem into smaller ones, figuring out what the simplest case is, and solving that manually.

Checking if one point is reachable from another

Context

Suppose from any given point (x,y), that you can make two types of moves. Either to move to (x,x+y), or (x+y,y).
For example, from (2,4) you can move to either (2,6), or (6,4).

You can move any number of times. For example: you can move from (2,6) to (2,8), then to (10,8), and finally to (18,8).

Task

Given two points (x,y) and (dx,dy) (dx denoting destination x) as 4 integers, write a recursive method that returns a boolean indicating whether it is possible to go from the first point to the second. For instance: from our earlier example, given the integers 2, 6, 18 and 8, the code should return true.

Your method should recursively compute whether the destination is reachable from the source and return true if it is, or false if not. Assume inputs are integers greater than or equal to 0. Ensure that you do not change the lines incrementing recursiveSteps.

More On Recursion

While recursive methods are intuitive and easy to implement, they can sometimes have performance issues due to excessive stack usage and slower execution. One technique to mitigate these issues is tail recursion.

Tail Recursion

Tail recursion is a special type of recursion where the recursive call is the last operation performed in the function, i.e., there are no pending operations or computations after the recursive call. This allows the compiler or interpreter to optimize the recursion by reusing the current stack frame instead of creating a new one for each recursive call.

Spoken_Languages_English_Disciplines_Mat.title: Recursion - Case Study (Math)
Spoken_Languages_English_Disciplines_Mat.description:
The Collatz Sequence | MATH

Context

You are a Math student who is studying number sequences and trying to find some interesting patterns.

You come across a sequence called the "Collatz sequence" or the "3n+1 sequence", in which each number in the sequence is defined by performing the following function to the previous number:

  • If the number is even, divide it by 2.
  • If the number is odd, multiply it by 3 and add 1.
For example: the sequence obtained using 5 as the starting digit is 5,16,8,4,2,1

You may notice that once the sequence reaches 1, it will go back to 4, then 2, and back to 1. Because of this cyclic property, 1 is seen as the endpoint for the sequence.

You then read about the Collatz conjecture, which asks whether all positive integers, no matter how large, eventually converge to 1. Even though this has been verified up to very large numbers, you want to explore the sequence yourself.

Task

Write a recursive function that prints the Collatz sequence starting from an integer n. Your program should:

  • Print each term in the sequence until the endpoint.
  • If n is less than or equal to 1, print n and return.

Sample Runs

Sample run 1: output of calling collatz(1)

1

Sample run 2: output of calling collatz(-2)

-2

Sample run 3: output of calling collatz(10)

10 5 16 8 4 2 1

Sample run 4: output of calling collatz(61)

61 184 92 46 23 70 35 106 53 160 80 40 20 10 5 16 8 4 2 1

Spoken_Languages_English_Disciplines_Sta.title: Recursion - Case Study (Statistics)
Spoken_Languages_English_Disciplines_Sta.description:
Binomial Coefficient | STATISTICS

Context

You are a Stats student who has come across a recursive definition of the Binomial Coefficient function i.e. n choose k, which is the number of ways to choose an unordered collection of k items from a collection of n items.

The formula is as follows:
C(n, k) = C(n − 1, k − 1) + C(n − 1, k), for all n and k such that 1 ≤ k ≤ n − 1.

It is also important to note:

  • C(n, 0) = 1 [intuition: there is only 1 way to choose 0 items from a list of n]
  • C(n, n) = 1 [intuition: there is only 1 way to choose n items from a list of n].

You want to test this recursive definition using a recursive function.

Task

Write a recursive function that prints the binomial coefficient of two integers n and k, such that 1 ≤ k ≤ n − 1. Your program should:

  1. For the cases mentioned above, return 1.
  2. Otherwise, if 1 ≤ k ≤ n − 1 is not true, return 0.
  3. Otherwise, compute the binomial coefficient recursively and return the result.

Sample Runs

Sample run 1 (n = 5, k = 0): output of calling binomialCoefficient(5,0)

1

Sample run 2 (n = 5, k = 5): output of calling binomialCoefficient(5,5)

1

Sample run 3 (n = -1, k = 5): output of calling binomialCoefficient(-1,5)

0

Sample run 4 (n = 5, k = 6): output of calling binomialCoefficient(5,6)

0

Sample run 5 (n = 7, k = 3): output of calling binomialCoefficient(7,3)

35

Sample run 6 (n = 7, k = 4): output of calling binomialCoefficient(7,4)

35

Binomial Coefficient | STATISTICS

Context

You are a Stats student who has come across a recursive definition of the Binomial Coefficient function i.e. n choose k, which is the number of ways to choose an unordered collection of k items from a collection of n items.

The formula is as follows:
C(n, k) = C(n − 1, k − 1) + C(n − 1, k), for all n and k such that 1 ≤ k ≤ n − 1.

It is also important to note:

  • C(n, 0) = 1 [intuition: there is only 1 way to choose 0 items from a list of n]
  • C(n, n) = 1 [intuition: there is only 1 way to choose n items from a list of n].

You want to test this recursive definition using a recursive function.

Task

Write a recursive function that prints the binomial coefficient of two integers n and k, such that 1 ≤ k ≤ n − 1. Your program should:

  1. For the cases mentioned above, return 1.
  2. Otherwise, if 1 ≤ k ≤ n − 1 is not true, return 0.
  3. Otherwise, compute the binomial coefficient recursively and return the result.

Introduction

In this lesson, we will look over some insights of Software Objects and Classes.

Objects

Objects, in general, represent entities in the real-world. In programming, an object has a similar notion; they have their own space in the memory to save their information. For example, a player in a game can be an object which stores information relevant to it such as health points, color, skills, etc.

Example

Can you spot the objects in the following image? How many are there?


There are a total of 6 objects in the image above. Each of these image occupy some space and have their unique properties such as color and shape.

Classes

Loosely speaking, classes are a collection of objects who share some common attributes.

Example

Can you look for classes in the following image?


There are multiple ways of defining classes in this context. One may categorize objects above on basis of their shape. In this case, we will have 3 classes namely Circle, Rectangle, and Triangle. What attributes/properties can you assign to these classes? (Hint: What is uncommon between the circle objects?)

Another way of defining classes coulde be on the basis of their color. We may define classes as Red, Green, and Blue. Here, the shape could be an attribute. Another way could be of simply defining one class: GeometricObjects with attributes as shape and color. This will enclose all the objects in the image.

So how should we define our classes? Defining classes complelety depends on the sitation and in practice, one should choose whichever feels most natural.

Classes to Objects

In programming, we define classes to classify different objects. The process of creating an object from a given class (like a blueprint) is called instantiating the class and the created object is called an instance of the class.

Following is an example which shows this conversion

Programming_Languages_Java_Spoken_Langua.body:
Static Modifiers

Static Modifiers determine what attributes/methods truly depend on the objects. To access any static attribute/method, we do not need to instantiate the class. To access them, we can simply use the . operator on the class name itself. For example, Math.pow(3,4). They are created using the static keyword.
  • static attributes: Shared by all the instances (objects) of the class. Thus, if we change the value of a static attribute of an object, then the value of that attribute will change for all instances of that class. In practice, it is recommended to change the value of static attribute using the class name instead of changing it through object reference.
    • Example:
    public class Car {
    public static int year = 2023; // this is a static attribute
}
  • static methods: Not tied to a specific object (they carry out a general function).
    • Example:
    public class Car {
    public static void avgSpeed() { // this is a static method
        System.out.println("Average speed of a car is 80mph"); 
    } 
}

Modificateurs Statiques

Les modificateurs statiques déterminent quels attributs/méthodes dépendent véritablement des objets. Pour accéder à n'importe quel attribut/méthode statique, nous n'avons pas besoin d'instancier la classe. Pour y accéder, nous pouvons simplement utiliser l'opérateur . sur le nom de la classe lui-même. Par exemple, Math.pow(3,4).

Ils sont créés en utilisant le mot clé static.

  • Attributs statiques : Partagés par toutes les instances (objets) de la classe. Ainsi, si nous changeons la valeur d'un attribut statique d'un objet, la valeur de cet attribut changera pour toutes les instances de cette classe. En pratique, il est recommandé de changer la valeur de l'attribut statique en utilisant le nom de la classe plutôt que de le faire par référence à l'objet.
    • Exemple :
    public class Car {
    public static int year = 2023; // ceci est un attribut statique
}
  • Méthodes statiques : Non liées à un objet spécifique (elles réalisent une fonction générale).
    • Exemple :
    public class Car {
    public static void avgSpeed() { // ceci est une méthode statique
        System.out.println("Average speed of a car is 80mph"); 
    } 
}

content.title: Object Oriented Programming B (Inheritance)

Programming_Languages_Java_Spoken_Langua.body:
Introduction

In this module, we will delve into the concept of inheritance, a powerful mechanism that establishes connections between classes. Just as we inherit certain traits from our parents in real life, in programming, classes are organized in a hierarchical structure to facilitate the sharing of properties and functionalities. Inheritance is usually established when there is a strong is-a type relation between child and parent.

Example

Consider the classes Circle, Rectangle, and Triangle. What common property do they share? They are all shapes and thus, we can define another class Shape which will have all the common attributes in Circle, Rectangle, and Triangle and these classes will simply be child classes of the parent Shape class. This is depicted by the following hierarchical diagram.

Here, Shape class is called the super class (or parent class) of its descendents and Circle, Rectangle, and Triangle classes are called the sub class (or child class) of its parent.

Remark. In Java, a class can have only one parent class.

What gets inherited?

Loosely speaking, almost all the properties (attributes and methods) of the parent class are inherited to the child class and these properties can either be used or modified in the child class. Thus, we may say that inheritance supports the notion of writing less and managable code as changing the definition of a certain attribute in parent class can likely make changes in child classes as well.

More specifically, all non-private instance variables are inherited along with all non-private methods. If we want to inherit an attribute/method while keeping it private, we use protected visibility modifier.

Method Overriding

Method overriding is a way that allows a subclass to provide a specific implementation of a method that is already defined in its superclass. This means that a subclass can have a method with the same name, return type, and parameters as in its superclass, but with a different implementation. Thus, loosely speaking, it helps us update the definition of an inherited method.

Example

Constructor Chaining

Constructor chaining in the context of inheritance refers to the process of calling a superclass constructor from a subclass constructor. When you create an object of a subclass, it contains the superclass part as well. To properly initialize both the subclass and superclass members, the subclass constructor needs to call the appropriate superclass constructor. This ensures that all members in the inheritance hierarchy are initialized correctly.

Spoken_Languages_English_Disciplines_Mat.description:
Polynomial Class

Context

You are a mathematician wanting to build a program for working with polynomials to automate some of your analysis. For this exercise, you are given a parent class called Polynomial, which represents a polynomial expression (i.e a mathematical expression consisting of variables and coefficients). The Polynomial class has no attributes and has two methods toString (or __str__ for Python), which returns the polynomial in standard form (eg: ax^2 + bx + c) as a string, and an evaluate() method, which returns the value after evaluating the polynomial for a given x.  

Task

Your task is to create two subclasses LinearPolynomial and QuadraticPolynomial that are intended to represent polynomials of their respective degrees.

  • Both subclasses should have the integer attributes for each coefficient (two coefficients for LinearPolynomial and three for QuadraticPolynomial).
  • Both subclasses should override and implement the two methods from the Polynomial class.
  • QuadraticPolynomial should also have a third method named hasRoots (or has_roots for Python) that returns a boolean value indicating whether the polynomial has real roots or not.

Note: Your constructors must accept coefficients in the same order as the standard standard (i.e. for a quadratic, order should be: a,b,c, corresponding to ax^2 + bx + c)

You do not need to create the main method, it has already been provided and is only for demonstration. The string representation must match the format of the examples below.

Sample Run

Linear Polynomial: 3x + 4
Evaluated at x = 2: 10

Quadratic Polynomial: 1x^2 + -4x + 3
Evaluated at x = 1: 0
Has roots? True

Spoken_Languages_English_Disciplines_Phy.title: OOP - Case Study (Physics)
Spoken_Languages_English_Disciplines_Phy.description:
Projectile Class

Context

You are given a parent class called Projectile, which represents a projectile launched into the air. The Projectile class has one attribute: initialVelocity (or initial_velocity, which represents the projectile's initial velocity (in m/s). The class also has a method for calculating the time of flight of the projectile if it was shot/thrown straight up with the specified initial velocity. You want to create classes to model a cannonball and an arrow, which are special cases of a projectile.

  • For the cannonball, picture a cannon on top of a cliff at a height of H, shooting a cannon with velocity v0. The cannon is not angled (i.e. the launch angle is zero and we will ignore it in this case).
  • For the arrow, picture an archer shooting an arrow at an angle θ. The archer is at ground level and the projectile flies through the air, landing back on the ground (i.e our initial and final heights are 0, and we will ignore them in this case).

For simplicity, we are ignoring air resistance.

Task

Your task is to create two subclasses Cannonball and Arrow that represent different types of projectiles.

  • Both subclasses should inherit the attribute for initial velocity from the Projectile class.
  • Both subclasses should override the method for calculating time of flight according to the formulas given below.
  • Each subclass should have additional attributes and methods as described below:
    • Cannonball:
      • Additional Attribute: height (the height from which the cannonball is launched in meters).
      • Method: calculateMaxDistance() - Calculates the maximum horizontal distance traveled by the cannonball.
    • Arrow:
      • Additional Attribute: launchAngle (the launch angle of the arrow in degrees ).
      • Method: calculateMaxHeight() - Calculates the maximum height attained by the arrow.

You do not need to create the main method, it has already been provided and is only for demonstration.

Formulas:
- Time of flight for Cannonball (seconds): sqrt(2 * H / g)
- Max Range for Cannonball (meters): v0 * timeOfFlight
- Time of flight for Arrow (seconds): 2 * v0 * sin(θ) / g [this is simply timeOfFlight from the Projectile class multiplied by sin(θ)]
- Max Height for Arrow (meters): (v0 * sin(θ))2 / (2 * g) OR (v0 * sin(θ) * timeOfFlight) / 4

[NOTE: most built-in functions that calculate sin() require inputs in radians, so make sure you convert from degrees to radians as needed]

Sample Run

Cannonball:
Initial velocity: 20.0m/s
Launched from height: 15.0m
Time of flight: 1.74s
Max range: 35.0m

Arrow:
Initial velocity: 25.0m/s
Launched at angle: 30.0degrees
Time of flight: 2.55s
Max height: 8.0m

Spoken_Languages_English_Disciplines_Sta.title: OOP - Case Study (Statistics)
Spoken_Languages_English_Disciplines_Sta.description:
ProbabilityDistribution Class

Context

Being a Statistics student, you have learn about probability distributions. You want to write a program to model some basic probability distributions to gauge your understanding. For this exercise, you are given a parent class called ProbabilityDistribution, which has one attribute: parameters, which is an array of doubles/floats representing the parameters for the probability distribution. The class has methods for calculating the Probability Mass Function and Cumulative Distribution Function of an event X occurring. You want to create classes to model a Uniform Distribution and a Binomial Distribution.

For simplicity, we are considering only discrete probability distributions, and you can assume all events are integers.

Task

Your task is to create two subclasses UniformDistribution and BinomialDistribution that represent different types of probability distributions.

  • Both subclasses should inherit the attribute for parameters from the ProbabilityDistribution class.
    • The constructor for UniformDistribution should take arguments for a, minimum value and b, maximum value
    • The constructor for BinomialDistribution should take arguments for n, the number of experiments and p, probability of each event
  • Both subclasses should override the methods for calculating PMF and CDF according to the formulas given below.

You do not need to create the main method, it has already been provided and is only for demonstration.

Basic Definitions

  • Probability distributions are mathematical functions that output the probability of a particular event occurring out of all possible events.
  • An event can be discrete or continuous. For an event to be discrete, it means that there are countable or finitely many outcomes. For example, the outcome of a die roll can be a whole number from 1-6, but cannot be 1.318, for instance. The number of people in an office, the outcome of a coin flip, yes/no, are all discrete values.
  • The Probability Mass Function (PMF) of a discrete probability distribution is the probability of an event happening. Eg: if a dice is rolled, the PMF of getting any number is 1/6
  • The Cumulative Distribution Function (CDF) of a discrete probability distribution is the cumulative probability of all events up to and including a particular event. Eg: if a die is rolled, the probability of getting a 3 or below = CDF(3) = the sum of all individual PMFs from 1-3.
  • A Discrete Uniform Distribution is where all events in an interval are equally likely. The parameters a and b represent the lower and upper bounds of the interval. Eg: the probability of picking any card out of a deck of 52 is said to follow a uniform distribution with a=1 and b=52.
  • A Binomial Distribution models a situation where the same experiment is repeated n times, and each time the probability of the particular event occurring is p. Eg: the number of Heads out of 3 coin flips is said to follow a binomial distribution with n = 3 and p = 0.5 (head or tails).

Formulas:
- For a Uniform Distribution: PMF(X) = 1/(b-a), for all X between a and b (inclusive).
- For a Binomial Distribution: PMF(X) = binomialCoefficient(n,k) * px * (1-p)n-x
- CDF(X) of any discrete distribution is the sum of all PMF's from 0 to X.

Sample Run

PMF of Uniform Distribution with a = 0, b = 10 at x = 5: 0.1
CDF of Uniform Distribution with a = 0, b = 10 at x = 8: 0.8
PMF of Binomial Distribution with n = 10, p = 0.5 at x = 3: 0.1172
CDF of Binomial Distribution with n = 10, p = 0.5 at x = 5: 0.623

In the training quiz, you will have unlimited attempts. To receive your badge, you must pass 3/3 of the scenarios. The scenarios are all in their own function; don't worry about this now. We will learn about functions later. Your only task is to write the condition into the if- statements brackets as indicated by the comments. 

Scenario 1: Online Shop Tax Calculation

Write a function to calculate the final price of an item after tax. If the customer is from "StateA", apply a 5% tax; if they're from "StateB", apply a 10% tax. If the customer is a registered member, apply an additional 2% discount after the tax. E.g. In the scenario, a customer is from "StateB" and IS registered, their overall tax should calculate to 108%.


Scenario 2: Library Management


Write a function to determine if a user can borrow a book from a library. A user can borrow a book if they have a valid membership and less than 3 books checked out. If the user is a premium member, they can have up to 5 books checked out.


Scenario 3: Smart Thermostat


Write a function for a smart thermostat. If the mode is set to "auto", check the current temperature. If the temperature is below 18°C, turn the heating on; if it's above 25°C, turn the cooling on. If the mode is "manual", take no action.

A vending machine uses codes ('A', 'B', 'C') to dispense different snacks. Write a function that takes a character code and returns the name of the snack.

- Case A should return “Chips”

- Case B should return “Chocolate”

- Case C Should Return “Cookie”

- If an invalid selection is made, the switch statement should return “Invalid Selection”


Scenario 2: Traffic Light Controller

Given an integer representing a traffic light state (1 for green, 2 for yellow, 3 for red), write a function that returns the action a driver should take.

- Case 1 should return “Go”

- Case 2 should return “Caution”

- Case 3 Should Return “Stop”

- If an invalid selection is made, the switch statement should return “Invalid Light”


Scenario 3: Day of the Week

Given an integer (1-7) representing days of the week, write a function that returns the name of the day.

- Case 1 should return “Monday”

- Case 2 should return “Tuesday”

- Case 3 Should Return “Wednesday”

- Case 4 should return “Thursday”

- Case 5 should return “Friday”

- Case 6 Should Return “Saturday”

- Case 7 Should Return “Sunday”

- If an invalid selection is made, the switch statement should return “Invalid Day”

Programming_Languages_Java_Spoken_Langua.body:
Introduction

Dans cette leçon, nous allons examiner le concept de gestion des exceptions. De nombreuses fois, lors du travail sur une base de code, nous rencontrons des erreurs qui doivent être corrigées soit par débogage, soit en gérant l'erreur de manière appropriée.

La gestion des exceptions permet à un programme de faire face à des situations exceptionnelles et de continuer son exécution normale. Une exception est un objet qui représente une erreur ou une condition empêchant l'exécution de se dérouler normalement. Lorsqu'une erreur est détectée, le flux normal du code s'arrête et cet objet d'exception est créé. Toutes les exceptions standard en Java sont des sous-classes de la classe Throwable.

Introduction

In this lesson, we will look over the concept of Exception Handling. 

Exception handling is a crucial concept in programming that deals with the management of errors and unusual conditions that may arise during the execution of a program. It provides a structured way to detect and respond to runtime anomalies, allowing the program to handle these issues gracefully without crashing. By using exception handling, developers can ensure their programs can manage unexpected events and maintain smooth operation.

Exception handling enables a program to deal with exceptional situations and continue its normal execution. An exception is an object that represents an error or a condition that prevents execution from proceeding normally. When an error is detected, the normal flow of the code stops and this exception objected is created. All standard exceptions in C++ are sub-classes of exception class.

En Java, vous pouvez également déclarer qu'une méthode pourrait lancer un type spécifique d'exception en utilisant le mot-clé throws dans la signature de la méthode.

            public void someMethod() throws SomeException {
                // Code de la méthode qui pourrait lever SomeException
            }

Programming_Languages_Python_Spoken_Lang.body: Similar to Java, the sequence of except statements matters. The first polymorphically matching except block is executed, and subsequent ones are skipped.
Tout comme en Java, l'ordre des déclarations except est important. Le premier bloc except correspondant polymorphiquement est exécuté, et les suivants sont ignorés.

Programming_Languages_C++_Spoken_Languag.body:
2. Declaring Exceptions

In Java, you can also declare that a method might throw a specific type of exception using the throws keyword in the method signature.

            void someMethod() throw(myExc) {
                // Method code that might throw SomeException
            }

2. Déclaration des exceptions

En Java, vous pouvez également déclarer qu'une méthode pourrait lever un type spécifique d'exception en utilisant le mot-clé throws dans la signature de la méthode.

            void someMethod() throws myExc {
                // Code de la méthode qui pourrait lever myExc
            }
Unlike Java, there is no compile time validation on putting the call of these error declaring functions in try-catch blocks and thus, exception declaration is not a recommended practice in C++.

Contrairement à Java, il n'y a pas de validation au moment de la compilation pour mettre l'appel de ces fonctions déclarant des erreurs dans des blocs try-catch et donc, la déclaration d'exception n'est pas une pratique recommandée en C++.

Programming_Languages_Python_Spoken_Lang.body: Unlike Java, there is no concept of exception declaration in Python.
Contrairement à Java, il n'y a pas de concept de déclaration d'exception en Python.

Programming_Languages_Java_Spoken_Langua.body: Important: When you call a method that declares an exception using throws, you must either enclose the method call in a try-catch block or declare the exception in the method's own throws clause. One can think of try-catch as an exception resolver and throws as an exception passer which is later on handled by a try-catch (or thrown to OS in which case the code might crash).

Important : Lorsque vous appelez une méthode qui déclare une exception à l'aide de throws, vous devez soit entourer l'appel de méthode dans un bloc try-catch, soit déclarer l'exception dans la clause throws de la méthode elle-même. On peut considérer try-catch comme un résolveur d'exceptions et throws comme un passeur d'exceptions qui sera ensuite géré par un bloc try-catch (ou jeté vers le système d'exploitation, auquel cas le code pourrait planter).

Checked and Unchecked Exceptions

The built-in exceptions can be categorized as

  • Checked Exceptions: These exceptions are compile-time exception i.e., they are checked by the complier during complilation time. For the code to complie successfully, it is important to handle these exceptions in the code properly.
  • Unchecked Exceptions: These exceptions are run-time exceptions i.e., they may occur when the code is executing. This can happen due to issues like bad input, division by zero, etc. As the complier does not check for these exceptions, we do not need to handle them until really required.

Exceptions vérifiées et non vérifiées

Les exceptions intégrées peuvent être catégorisées comme suit :

Spoken_Languages_French.body:
Introduction

Dans ce module, nous plongerons dans le concept de Polymorphisme, ce qui signifie plusieurs formes.

Comme discuté dans les modules précédents, une classe définit un type. Pour un type donné, nous définissons son supertype comme le type de sa super classe et son subtype comme le type de sa sous-classe (s'il y en a une). Le polymorphisme traite de la référence à un type avec son supertype.

Exemple

Considérons les classes Circle, Rectangle et Triangle, toutes étendant Shape. Ainsi, nous pouvons dire que tous les cercles sont des formes, tous les rectangles sont des formes, et tous les triangles sont aussi des formes. En contexte de programmation, ceci est vrai en raison du chaînage de constructeurs comme discuté dans le module précédent. Pour instancier un Circle, nous instancions d'abord un Shape et donc, tout objet de type Circle est aussi de type Shape.

Cette notion peut être généralisée comme suit : Chaque type est également un type de son supertype (s'il y en a un). Notez que la réciproque n'est pas vraie. Toutes les formes ne sont pas des cercles.

Spoken_Languages_English.body:
Introduction

In this module, we will delve into the concept of Polymorphism, which means multiple forms.

As discussed in previous modules, a class defines a type. For a given type, we define its supertype as the type of its super class and subtype as the type of its subclass (if any). Polymorphism deals with referencing a type with its supertype.

Example

Consider the classes Circle, Rectangle, and Triangle all of which extends Shape. Thus, we can say that all circles are shapes, all rectangles are shapes, and all triangles are shapes as well. In context of programming, this holds true because of constructor chaining as discussed in previous module. To instantitate Circle, we first instantitate Shape and thus, any object of type Circle is also of type Shape.

This notion can be generalized as: Every type is also a type of its supertype (if any). Note that the converse is not true. Not all shapes are circles.

This comprehensive lesson will guide you through the fundamental concepts of both loops and arrays in programming. We will delve into two essential aspects: the implementation of various types of loops and the effective use of arrays.

In C++, the 'for' loop is a control structure used to execute a block of code repeatedly for a specified number of times. It's particularly effective when the number of iterations is known before entering the loop. The 'for' loop offers a concise way to iterate over a range of values. It is often used for various programming tasks like array manipulation, algorithm implementation, and more.

 

How to Use For Loops

A 'for' loop in C++ typically includes three components:

Initialization: Here, you declare and initialize one or more loop control variables. It's executed only once at the beginning of the loop.

Condition: This is a boolean expression that is evaluated before each iteration of the loop. As long as this condition remains true, the loop continues to execute.

Increment/Decrement (Update): After each iteration of the loop body, this statement is executed, which usually modifies the loop control variable. It can increment or decrement the variable, or even change it in more complex ways.

'Do-while' loops serve a unique purpose in iterative control structures. Unlike 'for' and 'while' loops where the condition is tested at the beginning, in 'do-while' loops, the condition is evaluated after the loop body has executed. This ensures that the loop body is executed at least once, making 'do-while' loops ideal for situations where the loop must run at least once regardless of the condition.

 

How to Use Do-While Loops

The structure of a 'do-while' loop in C++ is straightforward and consists of two main parts:

 

Loop Body: This is the block of code that will be executed in each iteration of the loop. It's guaranteed to run at least once, regardless of the condition.

 

Condition: After the loop body is executed, this boolean expression is evaluated. If the condition is true, the loop will execute again. If it's false, the loop terminates.

Arrays are especially useful when you need to manage a list of items, such as numbers or characters, where each element can be efficiently accessed by its index. The concept of indexing and the nature of arrays are crucial to understanding how to store, access, and manipulate data in C++.

Write a Java function to add two 3x3 matrices. Each element in one matrix should be added to the corresponding element in the second matrix, and the result should be stored in a new 3x3 matrix.

Scenario 2: Transpose of a Matrix
Develop a Java function that calculates the transpose of a 3x3 matrix. The transpose is achieved by flipping the matrix over its diagonal such that the row and column indices of the elements are swapped.

Create a Java function to determine whether a 3x3 matrix is symmetric. A matrix is considered symmetric if it is equal to its transpose. In other words, the matrix should not change if you swap the rows with columns.

Programming_Languages_Python_Spoken_Lang.body:
Naming Conventions

Names used for classes, functions, and variables are called identifiers. When naming your components, you must follow a few rules:

  • An identifier must contain only letters (A to Z or a to z), numbers (0 to 9), and underscore (_).
  • All identifiers must start with a letter or _.
  • A keyword cannot be used as an identifier. For example, you can not name your variable if.
  • An identifier can be of any length.
  • Python is case-sensitive. This means the identifier print() is not the same as Print() or PRINT().

Examples:

  • Valid identifiers:
    • my_1st_name
    • myAge2.
  • Invalid identifiers:
    •  2go (invalid first character: shouldn't be a number)
    •  my-name (invalid character: -)
    •  my Age (invalid character: the space)

There are also conventions that are recommended when choosing identifiers:

  • Functions and variable names should start with a lower case letter.
  • If you use several words to form a name, use an underscore to separate them.

Examples:

  • my_age, interest_value
  • print()

Naming Conventions

Names used for classes, methods, and variables are called identifiers. When naming your components, you must follow a few rules:

  • An identifier must contain only letters (A to Z or a to z), numbers (0 to 9), underscore (_) and dollar sign ($).
  • All identifiers must start with a letter, _, or $.
  • A keyword cannot be used as an identifier. For example, you can not name your class if.
  • An identifier can be of any length.
  •  Java is case-sensitive. This means the identifier println() is not the same as Println() or PRINTLN().

Examples:

  • Valid identifiers:
    • my_1st_name
    • myAge2.
  • Invalid identifiers:
    •  2go (invalid first character: shouldn't be a number)
    •  my-name (invalid character: -)
    •  my Age (invalid character: the space)

There are also conventions that are recommended when choosing identifiers:

  • Method and variable names should start with a lower case letter. Class names should start with an upper case letter.
  • If you use several words to form a name, start each inner word with an upper case letter.

Examples:

  • class FirstProgram{...}
  • void main(...)
  • myAge, interestRate

Conventions de dénomination

Les noms utilisés pour les classes, les méthodes et les variables sont appelés identifiants. Lorsque vous nommez vos composants, vous devez suivre quelques règles :

  • Un identifiant ne doit contenir que des lettres (A à Z ou a à z), des nombres (0 à 9), trait de soulignement (_) et le signe dollar ($).
  • Tous les identifiants doivent commencer par une lettre, _, ou $.
  • Un mot-clé ne peut pas être utilisé comme identifiant. Pour exemple, vous pouvez ne pas nommer votre classe if.
  • Un identifiant peut avoir n'importe quelle longueur.
  • Java est sensible à la casse. Cela signifie que l'identifiant println() n'est pas le même que Println() ou PRINTLN().

Exemples :

  • Identifiants valides :
    • my_1st_name
    • monAge2.
  • Identifiants non valides :
    • 2go (premier caractère non valide : ne doit pas être un chiffre)
    • my-name (caractère non valide : -)
    • my Age (caractère non valide : l'espace)

Il existe également des conventions qui sont recommandé lors du choix des identifiants :

  • Les noms de méthode et de variable doivent commencer par une lettre minuscule. Classer les noms doivent commencer par une lettre majuscule.
  • Si vous utilisez plusieurs mots pour former un nom, commencez chaque mot intérieur par un lettre majuscule.

Exemples :

Spoken_Languages_French.body:
Dans cette leçon, vous découvrirez variables, constantes et types de données. Mais avant cela, vous devez connaître quelques notions de base sur la manière dont les données sont stockées dans la mémoire de l'ordinateur.

Une mémoire d'ordinateur (RAM) consiste en une séquence d'emplacements de mémoire pour stocker des programmes et des données. Chaque emplacement dispose d'un adresse numérique unique qui commence à 0. Vous pouvez considérer la mémoire comme une commode où chaque tiroir représente un emplacement mémoire. Supposons maintenant que vous donniez un numéro unique à chaque tiroir pour indiquer son emplacement ; le premier tireur reçoit le numéro 0, le second le 1, et ainsi de suite. Une adresse mémoire dans ce cas serait le numéro que vous attribuez à chaque tiroir.

Pourquoi avons-nous besoin de mémoire informatique ? Comme indiqué ci-dessus, la mémoire de l'ordinateur stocke les programmes et les données. Lorsque vous démarrez un programme, le programme est d'abord chargé dans la mémoire avant son exécution. Cela améliore les performances d'exécution. Après le démarrage de l'exécution, le programme peut sauvegarder et restaurer les données de la mémoire.

Comment tout cela est-il lié aux variables ? Le programme doit identifier où les données sont stockées dans la mémoire. Cela peut être fait en utilisant des adresses mémoire. Un moyen plus simple consiste à étiqueter ces emplacements de mémoire et à utiliser ces étiquettes lors de l'accès aux données. Pensez à étiqueter les emplacements de mémoire comme mettre un autocollant sur un tiroir avec un nom, comme dans l'exemple ci-dessous. Lorsque vous faites référence à ce tiroir, vous pouvez dire tiroir #3 ou tiroir Adam . Une variable est un nom que vous donnez à un emplacement mémoire dans votre programme.

Remarque : dans certains cas, un compilateur d'optimisation peut stocker une variable dans une mémoire spéciale appelée registre. Cependant, cela dépasse le cadre de cette introduction leçon.

In this lesson, you will learn about variables, constants, and data types. But before we do that, you need to know a few basics about how data is stored in the computer's memory.

A computer's memory (RAM) consists of a sequence of memory locations for storing programs and data. Each location has a unique numeric address which starts from 0. You can think of memory as a chest of drawers where each drawer represents one memory location. Now assume you give a unique number to each drawer to indicate its location; the first drawer gets the number 0, the second gets 1, and so on. A memory address in this case would be the number you give to each drawer.

Why do we need computer memory? As indicated above, computer memory stores programs and data. When you start a program, the program is first loaded into the memory before it is executed. This improves the execution performance. After execution starts, the program can save and restore data from the memory. 

How is this all related to variables? The program needs to identify where the data is stored in the memory. This can be done using memory addresses. An easier way is to label those memory locations and using these labels when accessing data. Think of labeling memory locations as putting a sticker on a drawer with a name, as in the example below. When referring to that drawer, you can either say drawer #3 or Adam's drawer. A variable is a name you give to a memory location in your program.

Note: in some cases, an optimizing compiler may store a variable in a special memory called a register. However, this is beyond the scope of this introductory lesson.

Java has two groups of data types: Primitives and Objects. At this point, we will focus primarily on primitives, while objects will be discussed in details later.

Primitive Datatypes

A primitive datatype specifies the memory size of a variable and the valid range of values a variable can store. For example, by indicating that x is of the type int in the examples in the previous section, the compiler reserves 4 bytes of memory for x, and it will only allow storing integers (whole numbers) that are restricted to the range indicated in the table below.

Type Casting

La conversion de type fait référence à la conversion de données d'un type (entier, flottant, etc.) en un autre. Nous avons deux types de casting : implicite et explicite.

Spoken_Languages_English.body:
Type Casting

Type casting refers to converting data from one type (integer, float, etc.) to another. We have two types of casting: implicit and explicit.

Programming_Languages_Python_Spoken_Lang.body:
Transformation de type implicite

Le casting implicite se produit automatiquement sans l'intervention du programmeur. La conversion n'entraîne pas la perte du sens d'origine ou précision des données.

Exemple

Dans la troisième instruction ci-dessous, nous voulons calculer 2 + 1.5 et stockez le résultat dans res. Python va convertir automatiquement la valeur 2 du plus petit type au plus grand type, donc 2 devient 2.0 qui est ensuite ajouté à 1.5 résultant en 2.5. Par conséquent, le type de res serait float. Notez que le type de n et f ne le font pas changer.

Implicit Type Casting

Implicit casting happens automatically without the programmer's involvement. The conversion does not lead to losing the original meaning or precision of the data.

Example

In the third statement below, we want to compute 2 + 1.5 and store the result in res. Python will automatically convert the value 2 from the smaller type to the larger type, so 2 becomes 2.0 which is then added to 1.5 resulting in 2.5. Therefore, the type of res would be float. Note that the type of n and f do not change.

Programming_Languages_Java_Spoken_Langua.body:

Implicit casting happens automatically without the programmer's involvement. The conversion does not lead to losing the original meaning or precision of the data.

Example

In the second statement below, we want to store the integer value 2 (4 bytes, no decimals) into a double variable d (8 bytes, with decimals). Therefore, Java will automatically convert the value 2 from the smaller type to the larger type (this is called type widening), so 2 becomes 2.0.

Explicit Type Casting

Explicit casting is done manually by the programmer who has to add extra code to change the datatype. Here, loss of data may occur as the programmer forces data to a specific type. The syntax is:

<required_type> (data)

where <required_type> is a predefined function such as  int(), float(), str(),  etc.

Example

In the second statement below, we want to add the value 3 stored as a string in n2 to the integer 2. Python will not automatically convert a string (higher type) to an integer (lower type). Therefore, you will have to explicitly convert this the string "3" to integer 3 using the int() function. If you replace res = n1 + int(n2) with res = n1 + n2, you will get a TypeError.

Programming_Languages_Java_Spoken_Langua.body:
Explicit Type Casting

Explicit casting is done manually by the programmer who has to add extra code to change the datatype. Here, loss of data may occur as the programmer forces data to a specific type. The syntax is:

( <required_type> ) data

where <required_type> is the required primitive type, e.g. int, double, char,  etc.

Example

In the second statement below, we want to store the double value 2.25 (8 bytes, with decimals) into an integer variable n (4 bytes, no decimals). A variable can only hold values of its own type. Since converting 2.25 will lead to data loss (i.e., losing the decimals), you will have to explicitly convert this value from the larger type to the smaller type (this is called type narrowing), so 2.25 becomes 2.

Spoken_Languages_English.body:
Introduction

We can use operators to perform certain operations on values and variables.

In the example below, we use the addition operator (+) to add together the values 5 and 7, resulting in the value 12. Then, we use the assignment operator (=) to assign the result (i.e. 12) to sum.

Spoken_Languages_French.body:
Présentation

Nous pouvons utiliser des opérateurs pour effectuer certaines opérations sur des valeurs et des variables.

Dans l'exemple ci-dessous, nous utilisons l'opérateur d'addition (+) additionner les valeurs 5 et 7, résultant en la valeur 12. Ensuite, on utilise le opérateur d'affectation (=) pour affecter le résultat (c'est-à-dire 12) à sum.

Spoken_Languages_English.body:
In this section, we will discuss the following operators:

  • Simple Assignment operator
  • Arithmetic operators
  • Relational operators
  • Logical operators
  • Bitwise operators

We will also discuss some shortcuts that may be used in your code.

Spoken_Languages_French.body:
Dans cette section, nous aborderons les opérateurs suivants :

  • Simple Assignment operator
  • Arithmetic operators

Nous discuterons également de certains raccourcis pouvant être utilisés dans votre code.

Opérateur d'affectation simple

Les opérateurs d'affectation, en général, affectent des valeurs aux variables. Un opérateur d'affectation simple = attribue la valeur sur le côté droit de l'opérateur à une variable sur le côté gauche.

Exemple

Dans la première instruction de l'exemple ci-dessous, la valeur 5 (à droite) est attribué à x (à gauche). Dans le deuxième énoncé, l'expression x + 3 est calculé en premier, puis le résultat, qui est 8, est attribué à o.

Spoken_Languages_English.body:
Simple Assignment Operator

Assignment operators, in general, assign values to variables. A simple assignment operator = assigns the value on the right hand side of the operator to a variable on the left hand side.

Example

In the first statement of the example below, the value 5 (on the right) is assigned to x (on the left). In the second statement, the expression x + 3 is computed first then the result, which is 8, is assigned to y.

Spoken_Languages_English.body:
As you can see, the value of x at the end was 7. Don't let this confuse you. The = operator in programming is not the same as the mathematical equal sign. Instead, it is a computer operation that assigns the value on the right to the variable on the left. The way we use variables depend on where it is located with respect to the = operator:

  • If a variable is located on the right of =, we substituted it with its current value.
  • If a variable is located on the left of f = , we use it to store the value from the right hand side of = .

In the statement x = x + 2, the value of the expression x + 2 on the right is computed first with the existing value of x, which is 5, resulting in the value 7. This result is then assigned to the same variable x, because it is now located on the left, updating its value to 7.

Spoken_Languages_French.body:
Comme vous pouvez le voir, la valeur de x à la fin était 7. Ne laissez pas cela vous confondre. Le = L'opérateur en programmation n'est pas le même que le signe égal mathématique. À la place, c'est une opération informatique qui attribue la valeur à droite au variables à gauche. La façon dont nous utilisons les variables dépend de l'endroit où elles se trouvent par rapport à l'opérateur = :

  • Si une variable est située à droite de =, nous l'avons remplacé par sa valeur actuelle.
  • Si une variable est située à gauche de f = , nous l'utilisons pour stocker la valeur du côté droit de = .

Dans la déclaration x = x + 2, la valeur du l'expression x + 2 à droite est calculée en premier avec la valeur existante de x, qui est 5, résultant en la valeur 7. Ce résultat est ensuite affecté à la même variable x, car elle se trouve maintenant à gauche, mettant à jour son valeur à 7.

Programming_Languages_Python_Spoken_Lang.body:
Increment and Decrement Operators

Unlike other languages, Python does not have increment ++ or decrement -- operators. These operators are used to increment or decrement a variable by 1. If you want to do this in Python, you need to write x += 1 or x = x + 1 to increment a variable x by 1, and x -= 1 or x = x - 1 to decrement x by 1.

If you want to learn about these operators and how they are used, please switch the lesson configuration options to another language (e.g. Java).

Opérateurs d'incrémentation et de décrémentation

Contrairement à d'autres langages, Python n'a pas d'incrément ++ ou décrémenter -- les opérateurs. Ces opérateurs permettent d'incrémenter ou de décrémenter une variable de 1. Si vous voulez faire cela en Python, vous devez écrire x += 1 ou x = x + 1 pour incrémenter un variable x par 1, et x -= 1 ou x = x - 1 pour décrémenter x par 1.

Si vous souhaitez en savoir plus sur ces opérateurs et sur leur utilisation, veuillez basculez les options de configuration de la leçon vers une autre langue (par exemple, Java).

Programming_Languages_Java_Spoken_Langua.body:
Opérateurs d'incrémentation et de décrémentation

Il existe de nombreuses situations dans lesquelles vous devrez incrémenter ou décrémenter une variable de 1 (comme vous le verrez plus tard). Vous pouvez déjà faites-le en utilisant ce que vous avez appris jusqu'à présent, par ex. en utilisant x += 1 ou x = x + 1.

Cependant, un moyen encore plus court consiste à utiliser l'incrément ++ et les opérateurs de décrémentation --. Par exemple, x++ (prononcé x plus plus) signifie incrémenter x de 1. Vous pouvez également utiliser ++x pour incrémenter x de 1.

int x = 5 ;
x++ ; //x vaut maintenant 6. C'est appelé incrément de suffixe
++x ; //x est maintenant 7. C'est ce qu'on appelle incrément de préfixe

Maintenant, vous vous demandez peut-être quelle est la différence entre le suffixe et incrémentation (ou décrémentation) du préfixe ? Pour l'exemple ci-dessus, il n'y a pas différence. Cependant, il y a une différence si vous utilisez ces opérateurs dans des instructions qui font plus que de simples opérations d'incrémentation ou de décrémentation. La le tableau ci-dessous montre cette différence pour le ++ opérateur; le -- fonctionne de la même manière sauf que il décrémente la valeur de 1.

Raccourci Signification Exemple
x++ Incrément de suffixe : utilisez la valeur d'origine de x dans l'instruction incrémente alors x de 1. int x = 5 ; //x vaut 5
v = x++ ; //v est assigné 5, alors x devient 6
System.out.print(x++); //imprime 6, alors x devient 7
++x Incrément de préfixe : incrément x par 1 utilisez d'abord la nouvelle valeur dans l'instruction. int x = 5 ; //x vaut 5
v = ++x ; //x devient 6, alors v se voit attribuer 6
System.out.print(++x); //x devient 7, puis imprime 7

Exemple

int x = 10, y = 10 ;
int z = x++ * ++y ;
System.out.print(x); //imprime 11
System.out.print(y); //imprime 11
System.out.print(z); //imprime 110 (c'est-à-dire 10 * 11)

Increment and Decrement Operators

There are many situations where you will need to increment or decrement a variable by 1 (as you will see later). You can already do this using what you learned so far, e.g. using x += 1 or x = x + 1.

However, an even shorter way is to use the increment ++ and decrement -- operators. For example, x++ (pronounced x plus plus) means increment x by 1. You can also use ++x to increment x by 1.

int x = 5;
x++;    //x is now 6. This is called postfix increment
++x;    //x is now 7. This is called prefix increment

Now you might be wondering, what is the difference between the postfix and prefix increment (or decrement)? For the above example, there is no difference. However, there is a difference if you using these operators in statements that do more than just increment or decrement operations. The table below shows that difference for the ++ operator; the -- works the same way except that it decrements the value by 1.

Shortcut Meaning Example
x++ Postfix increment: use original value of x in the statement then increment x by 1. int x = 5;             //x is 5
v = x++;               //v is assigned 5, then x becomes 6
System.out.print(x++); //print 6, then x becomes 7
++x Prefix increment: increment x by 1 first then use the new value in the statement. int x = 5;             //x is 5
v = ++x;               //x becomes 6, then v is assigned 6
System.out.print(++x); //x becomes 7, then print 7 

Example

int x = 10, y = 10;
int z = x++ * ++y;
System.out.print(x);  //prints 11
System.out.print(y);  //prints 11
System.out.print(z);  //prints 110 (i.e. 10 * 11)

Priorité des opérateurs

Lorsque vous avez une expression qui implique plusieurs opérateur, il est important de connaître l'ordre dans lequel les opérations sont effectué.

Par exemple, dans le code ci-dessous, la valeur de x est 11. Cette est parce que l'opérateur * a une priorité plus élevée que + ; c'est-à-dire qu'il doit être évalué en premier. Cette signifie que la déclaration ci-dessous est équivalente à x = 5 + (2 * 3).

Operator Precedence

When you have an expression that involves more than one operator, it is important to know the order in which the operations are performed.

For example, in the code below, the value of x is 11. This is because the * operator has higher precedence than +; i.e. it must be evaluated first. This means the statement below is equivalent to x = 5 + (2 * 3).

Spoken_Languages_French.body:
Exemple 1

Voyons comment l'expression x + y * 3 > 10 dans le code ci-dessous est imprimé false.

Spoken_Languages_English.body:
Example 1

Let's see how the expression x + y * 3 > 10 in the code below is prints false.

Programming_Languages_Python_Spoken_Lang.body:
x = 5; y = 1
print( x + y * 3 &gt 10)     # output: False

Programming_Languages_Java_Spoken_Langua.body:
int x = 5, y = 1;
System.out.println( x + y * 3 &gt 10); //output: false

int x = 5, y = 1;
System.out.println( x + y * 3 &gt 10); //production: false

Programming_Languages_Python_Spoken_Lang.body:
x = 5; y = 1
print( x + y * 3 &gt 10)     # production: False

Programming_Languages_C++_Spoken_Languag.body:
int x = 5, y = 1;
cout &lt&lt x + y * 3 &gt 10 &lt&lt endl; //output: false

int x = 5, y = 1;
cout &lt&lt x + y * 3 &gt 10 &lt&lt endl; //production: false

Spoken_Languages_French.body:
1. L'opérateur * a le plus haut priorité dans cette expression. Par conséquent, y * 3 est calculé en premier. Puisque y est 1, le résultat de y * 3 est 3.
  2. Maintenant, l'expression devient x + 3 > 10. L'opérateur + a une priorité plus élevée que l'opérateur >, donc x + 3 est ensuite calculé, ce qui donne 8.
  3. Maintenant, l'expression devient 8 > 10 qui est évalué à faux.

Exemple 2

L'opérateur d'affectation augmentée est exécuté en dernier après toute expression sur le droit est calculé. Dans le code ci-dessous, la valeur finale de x est 15. En effet, l'expression de droite est calculée en premier, ce qui donne la valeur 3. Ensuite, 3 est multiplié par la valeur actuelle de x et le résultat est stocké dans x.

Spoken_Languages_English.body:
1. The * operator has the highest precedence in this expression. Therefore, y * 3 is computed first. Since y is 1, the result of y * 3 is 3.
  2. Now the expression becomes x + 3 > 10. The + operator has a higher precedence than the > operator,  therefore x + 3 is computed next resulting in 8.
  3. Now the expression becomes 8 > 10 which is evaluated to false.

Example 2

The augmented assignment operator is performed last after any expression on the right is computed. In the code below, the final value of x is 15. This is because the expression on the right is computed first, resulting in the value 3. Then, 3 is multiplied by the current value of x and the result is stored in x.

Programming_Languages_Java_Spoken_Langua.body:
int x = 5;
x *= 2 + 1;             //same as x = x * (2+1)

x *= 2 + 1              # same as x = x * (2+1)

x = 5
x *= 2 + 1              # pareil que x = x * (2+1)
